svg.text: The same rule written in two places is not duplication: it is the difference between a good message and a guarantee. Only the database guarantees under concurrency.
Only an active enrollment can be transferred
Exactly one active enrollment per student and year
The academic year ends after it starts
One grade per enrollment, subject and term
One attendance row per enrollment and day
One closing per class group and term
A closed term refuses a grade posting
the same advisory lock, then isClosed() again
A closed year refuses a roll call
A batch names only this class group's active enrollments, once each
UNIQUE per day and per subject-and-term
A roll-call date is an ISO day that exists
Roll call within the class group's academic year
CPF: 11 digits with correct check digits
A guardian answers for a student only once
Passed = average ≥ minimum AND attendance ≥ minimum
PRIMARY KEY idempotent_request, claimed by the write's own transaction
A write carries the application's mark
Shape and type of every external input
12 invariants live in both places · 7 only the database guarantees · 5 only the domain knows · 2 the edge alone sees
Why write the same rule twice
The two sides do different jobs.
The domain predicate exists to give a MESSAGE. It runs first, knows
which field was wrong and returns a Result the screen can show next
to the input. A violated CHECK returns 23514 and a string nobody
The CHECK exists to give a GUARANTEE. It holds for the seed, for the
migration, for the SQL someone runs in psql at two in the morning
and for the version of the code not deployed yet. The predicate only
holds for whoever went through it.
Neither replaces the other. Removing the predicate makes the screen
worse; removing the CHECK erases the guarantee.
The Edge column is a third job again: zod does not know the rule, it
knows the shape. It is what keeps a string where a number was
expected from ever reaching a predicate that assumes a number.
What ONLY the database can guarantee
The rows with nothing in the Domain column have two things in
common: uniqueness and ordering. Neither survives concurrency when
Between the SELECT that says “it does not exist” and the INSERT that
creates it, a whole other transaction fits. Two simultaneous
enrollments for one student pass both checks and create both rows.
That is why active_enrollment_unique_per_year is an index and the
INSERT uses ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING: the clash is zero rows, not a
Ordering is the newer half. Closing a term and posting into it are
two transactions that used to overlap; pg_advisory_xact_lock on
(class_group_id, term) makes them take turns, and it is released by
the commit rather than by code that has to remember.
The same reasoning put the Idempotency-Key claim inside the write's
own transaction: exclusivity by PRIMARY KEY, atomicity by ROLLBACK.
isDateWithinAcademicYear — the database keeps the roll-call date and
the academic year dates in different tables; comparing them is a
rule, and a rule lives in a pure function.
allTermsClosed — “this year is over” is not a column either. It is
read out of four closing rows and used to refuse a roll call that
would move a report card nobody can correct any more.
finalStatus — passed or failed NEVER becomes a column (I5). Average,
attendance percentage and status are computed on read, from the
grades and the attendance. Storing the result would create a second
truth that goes stale on the first grade correction.
Announcement title and body, and the minimum password length:
product limits, which change by decision and not by integrity. A
migration to loosen a text limit is cost with nothing in return.
Invariants read from apps/api/src/*/domain/, apps/api/src/shared/ and migrations/0001_initial_schema.sql. State of Stage 01.
